summary: This informational RFC discusses the sanctions that could be applied to violators of IETF intellectual property rights policy, who applies them and how, to reduce ambiguity.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF's rules say that if you know about a patent or other intellectual property that matters for the work you are contributing, you have to disclose it. This RFC lists what happens when someone does not, and who decides. It also says what a sanction can never do: it cannot delete your name from a document you wrote unless your text goes too.

questions: what happens if someone violates ietf ipr policy
what sanctions exist for ipr disclosure violations
what is a posting rights action
who applies ipr sanctions in the ietf
subtitle: What the IETF does when a participant does not disclose intellectual property that matters for the work.

tldr.problem: The IETF's intellectual property rules make each participant responsible for disclosing relevant IPR, and the rules say nothing about what happens when someone does not.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC restates the disclosure obligation, explains who acts on a complaint, and lists ten administrative sanctions in approximate order of severity, from a private conversation to a Posting Rights Action that removes mailing list posting rights for a year.
tldr.outcome: All the sanctions listed are already available in existing IETF processes, and at least two IPR policy violations had been handled using some of them by the time the RFC was written.

facts.label: Posting Rights Action
facts.value: Posting rights removed for a year, unless revoked or extended

facts.label: Disclosure conditions
facts.value: 3: awareness, relevance to the work, and ownership

today: RFC 6701 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It summarizes the policy set out in RFC 3979 rather than replacing it, so the policy itself still has to be read in that document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IETF has developed and documented policies that govern the behaviour of all IETF participants with respect to intellectual property about which they might reasonably be aware. These are documented in RFC 3979 and are frequently brought to the attention of IETF participants. This document summarizes and references those policies but does not replace or stand in for the full statement of the policies found in RFC 3979; readers and participants need to be aware of the content of that document.

The policies state that each individual participant is responsible for disclosing, or ensuring the disclosure of, Intellectual Property Rights where all of the following apply: they are aware of the IPR, the IPR is relevant to the IETF work they are participating in, and the IPR is owned by the individual or by a company that employs or sponsors the individual's work.

This document discusses these issues and provides a suite of potential actions that can be taken within the IETF community in cases related to patents. All of these sanctions are currently available in IETF processes, and at least two instances of violation of the IPR policy had been handled using some of the sanctions listed. As explicitly called out in Section 4, a posting rights action is an applicable sanction for a breach of the IETF's IPR policy.

The document specifies some administrative sanctions that can be imposed by and through IETF administrative processes. It does not address or limit other legal sanctions, rights or remedies that are available outside of the IETF, or any of the legal rights or remedies that anyone has regarding IPR. It also does not consider the parallel but important issue of ways to actively promote conformance with the IETF's IPR policy, which is discussed in RFC 6702.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF's rules say that if you know about a patent or other intellectual property that matters for the work you are contributing, you have to disclose it. This RFC lists what happens when someone does not, and who decides.

sections.title: The IETF IPR Policy
sections.content:
Nothing in this document defines or redefines the IETF's IPR policy; this section highlights some important aspects of it. Individual participants have a personal responsibility to disclose, or ensure the timely disclosure of, IPR of which they are aware and which they own, or which is owned by a company that employs or sponsors them, and which impinges upon the contribution they make to the IETF. A contribution is defined in RFC 3979 and includes Internet-Drafts, emails to IETF mailing lists, presentations at IETF meetings, and comments made at the microphone during IETF meetings. Remote participants are bound by that definition just as those taking part in person are.

The timeliness of disclosure matters. No precise definition of timeliness is given in RFC 3979, and it is not the purpose of this document to supply one, but the impact that an IPR disclosure has on the smooth working of the IETF is directly related to how late in the process the disclosure is made. A disclosure made on a published RFC is very likely to be more disruptive to the IETF than such a disclosure on an early revision of an individual submission of an Internet-Draft. Third-party disclosures can also be made by anyone who has cause to believe that IPR exists, and such disclosures must be accompanied by the reasons for them.

Each individual participant has a choice under the policy: if they are unwilling or unable to disclose the existence of relevant IPR in a timely manner, they have the option to refrain from contributing to and participating in IETF activities about the technology covered by the IPR.

The IETF draws attention to the policy through the 'Note Well' statement that appears on its web pages, in presentations at working group and plenary meetings, and in the boilerplate text appearing in each Internet-Draft and RFC. The Note Well statement is also accepted by any person signing up to join an email list hosted at ietf.org. The procedure for filing IPR disclosures is shown on the IETF's web site, third-party disclosures can also be made by email to the IETF Secretariat or via the web page, and early disclosures or warnings that there might be IPR on a technology can also be made.

When a working group is notified of the existence of IPR, it must decide whether to continue with the work as it is or to revise the work to try to avoid the IPR claim. That decision is made on the working group's mailing list using normal rough consensus procedures, but discussions of the applicability of an IPR claim, or of the appropriateness or merit of the IPR licensing terms, are outside the scope of the working group. The IPR situation is considered by working group participants as the document advances through the development process, in particular at key times such as adoption of the document by the working group and during last call.

It needs to be clearly understood that the way a working group handles an IPR disclosure is distinct from the sanctions that can be applied to the individuals who violated the policy. A decision by a working group to rework an Internet-Draft entirely in order to avoid a disclosed claim should not be seen as a sanction against the authors. Especially in the case of a late disclosure, a working group deciding to do this can be considered a harmful side effect on the working group, since it slows down the publication of an RFC and might derail other work, and it should be considered one of the reasons to apply sanctions to the individuals concerned.
sections.plainLanguage: How late a disclosure happens decides how much damage it does. A disclosure that lands after a document is published as an RFC is much harder for the working group to absorb than one that lands on an early draft. And a working group that rewrites a document to avoid a claim is not punishing the authors; it is cleaning up after the late disclosure.

sections.title: Who Initiates Sanctions
sections.content:
Any IETF participant can draw attention to an apparent violation of the IETF's IPR policy. This can be done by sending email with a short summary of the relevant facts and events to the appropriate IETF mailing list. Normally, the working group chairs and area directors assume the responsibility for ensuring the smooth running of the IETF and for the enforcement of IETF policies including the IPR policy. So when sanctions are appropriate, working group chairs will be the first actors when there is an active working group involved in the technical work, and area directors will be the first actors in other cases. The first step will usually be for the working group chairs or the area director to gather the facts and discuss the matter with the IETF participants involved.

Working group chairs are already empowered to take action against working group participants who flout the IPR rules and so disrupt the smooth running of the IETF or a specific working group, just as they can take such action in the face of other disruptions. The chairs have the responsibility to select the appropriate actions, since they are closest to the details of the issue. Where there is no working group involved, or where making the decision or applying the sanctions is uncomfortable or difficult for the working group chairs, the responsible area director is available to guide or direct the action if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can report a suspected violation. The working group chairs normally handle it, because they know the details; the area director steps in when there is no working group involved or when the chairs want cover for the decision.

sections.title: The Available Sanctions
sections.content:
Section 4 lists some of the sanctions available to handle the case of an individual who violates the IETF's IPR policies. It is not intended to be an exhaustive list, it is not suggested that only one sanction be applied in any case, and it is not suggested that every case of infringement is the same or that the severest sanctions may be applied in each case. In many cases it may be appropriate to notify a wider part of the IETF community of the violation and the sanctions, so that patterns of behaviour can be spotted and handled. The sanctions are listed in approximate order of severity, but the ordering should not be taken as definitive or as driving different decisions in different cases.

The ten sanctions are these. A private discussion between the working group chair or area director and the individual, to understand what went wrong and how it can be prevented in the future. A formal but private warning that the individual must improve their behaviour or risk one of the other sanctions. A formal warning on an IETF mailing list that the individual must improve their behaviour or risk one of the other sanctions. Announcement to the working group of the failure by the individual. Ongoing refusal to accept the individual as editor of any new working group documents, the appointment of editors being entirely at the discretion of the working group chairs acting for the working group. Removal of the individual as working group document editor on specific documents or across the whole working group. Re-positioning of the individual's attribution in a document to the 'Acknowledgements' section, with or without a note explaining why they are listed there and not in the 'Authors' Addresses' section, an action that can also be recorded by the area director in the Datatracker entries for the documents concerned. Deprecation or rejection of the individual document, whether it be an RFC or an Internet-Draft, or cessation of work on the affected technology. Application of a temporary suspension of the individual's posting rights to a specific mailing list according to the guidelines in RFC 2418, applied to specific individuals and individual working group mailing lists at the discretion of the working group chairs for a period of no more than 30 days. And the removal of posting privileges using a Posting Rights Action as per RFC 3683, a more drastic measure to be applied when other sanctions are considered insufficient or to have been ineffective.

A Posting Rights Action is introduced by an area director and is considered by the IETF community and the IESG in order to determine IETF consensus. When one is in place, the subjects have their posting rights to a particular IETF mailing list removed for a period of a year, unless the action is revoked or extended, and maintainers of any IETF mailing list may, at their discretion and without further recourse to explanation or discussion, also remove posting rights.

One limit applies to all of this. Individuals who have supplied text that is included in an IETF document have a right to be recognized for their contribution. Authors' names therefore cannot be entirely removed from a document when the individual violates the IPR policy, unless the text they contributed is also completely removed. A name can be removed from the front page and even moved out of the 'Authors' Addresses' section, so long as proper acknowledgement of the contribution is given in the 'Acknowledgements' section.

The RFC adds a note on the applicability of Posting Rights Actions. According to RFC 3683, a PR action may be considered as a practice for use by the IETF in the case that a participant has engaged in a denial-of-service attack to disrupt the consensus-driven process. In some cases, ignoring or flouting the IETF's IPR policy may be considered as disruptive to the smooth operation of a working group or of the whole IETF, such that the offender might be deemed to be a disruptive individual under the terms of RFC 2418 and RFC 3683, and so liable to be the subject of a sanction restricting their rights to post to IETF mailing lists.
sections.plainLanguage: The sanctions run from a private word to losing the right to post to mailing lists for a year. Two limits matter: a person's name cannot be deleted from a document they wrote unless their text is deleted too, and the list is not exhaustive, so more than one sanction can apply to the same case.

sections.title: Fairness, Appeals and Choosing a Sanction
sections.content:
As with all decisions made within the IETF, any person who feels that they have been subject to unfair treatment, or who considers that a decision has been made incorrectly, may appeal the decision. The IETF's appeals procedures are described in Section 6.5 of RFC 2026 and reinforced in the IESG statement on appeals, and any of the sanctions described may be appealed using these procedures.

Whoever is applying sanctions will want to be sure that the chosen sanction matches the severity of the offence and considers all circumstances. The judgment needs to be applied equitably, so that similar situations are treated similarly in the future. If in any doubt, the person selecting and applying the sanctions should seek the opinion of the relevant part of the IETF community or of the community as a whole, and should not hesitate to seek advice from colleagues such as co-chairs, area directors or the whole IESG.

Appendix A supplies a list of questions that might form part of that judgment. It is described as guidance, not prescriptive or exhaustive, and it implies no weighting of the considerations. The questions include how long the participant has been active in the IETF, whether there is some exceptional circumstance, and whether special circumstances imply that the individual would not have seen or understood the pointers to and content of RFC 3979. Further questions ask how late the disclosure is: whether the document is already a working group document, how many revisions have been published, how much time has elapsed, whether last calls have been held, and whether the work has been published as an RFC. The remaining questions ask whether the individual is a minor contributor to the IETF work or clearly a major contributor, whether there is a reason for the individual forgetting the existence of the IPR, whether the individual was told by their company that disclosure was imminent but then something different happened, how speedy and humble the individual's apology was, how disruptive to the IETF work the disclosure and the associated license terms are, with a factor being whether the IETF community sees the need to re-work the document, and whether the large number of patents the individual has invented provides any level of excuse for failing to notice that one of their patents covered the IETF work.
sections.plainLanguage: Any sanction can be appealed through the IETF's normal appeal process. Picking the right one is a judgment call, and the RFC offers a list of questions to help make that call, such as how late the disclosure was, whether the person apologised quickly, and how much work the disclosure caused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: While nothing in this document directly affects the operational security of the Internet, failing to follow the IETF's IPR policies can be disruptive to the IETF's standards development processes, and so may be regarded as an attack on the correct operation of the IETF. Furthermore, a late IPR disclosure, or a complete failure to disclose, could represent an attack on the use of deployed and operational equipment in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's point is that failing to disclose intellectual property is itself a form of attack, on the IETF's process and on the people who deploy the resulting standards.

viz.caption: WHO ACTS WHEN A VIOLATION IS REPORTED (RFC 6701)

messages.label: Report the violation
messages.note: Email with a short summary of the relevant facts and events.

messages.label: Seek guidance
messages.note: For cases with no working group, or where the decision is difficult.

messages.label: Introduce a PR action
messages.note: The most drastic sanction, considered by the community and the IESG for consensus.

viz.caption: THE TEN SANCTIONS, IN APPROXIMATE ORDER OF SEVERITY

cells: a. Private discussion
The chair or area director talks to the individual to understand what went wrong.
b. Private formal warning
A formal warning, kept private, that behaviour must improve.
c. Mailing list warning
A formal warning posted on an IETF mailing list.
d. Announcement to the working group
The failure is announced to the working group.
e. Refusal of editorship
The individual is not accepted as editor of new working group documents.
f. Removal as editor
The individual is removed as editor on specific documents or across the working group.
g. Re-positioned attribution
The name moves to the Acknowledgements section, optionally with a note explaining why.
h. Document deprecated or rejected
The document is deprecated or rejected, or work on the technology stops.
i. Temporary posting suspension
Posting rights to a specific mailing list are suspended for no more than 30 days.
j. Posting Rights Action
Posting rights to a particular mailing list are removed for a year. The most drastic measure.

viz.caption: QUESTIONS FROM APPENDIX A THAT GUIDE THE CHOICE

items.title: How late was the disclosure?
items.text: Is the document already a working group document, how many revisions have been published, and has last call been held?

items.title: What did the individual know?
items.text: Is there a reason for forgetting the IPR, or special circumstances that imply the pointers to RFC 3979 were never seen?

items.title: How large a contributor?
items.text: Is the individual a minor contributor to the IETF work, or clearly a major contributor?

items.title: How was the apology?
items.text: How speedy and humble was the individual's apology?

items.title: How disruptive was it?
items.text: How disruptive to the IETF work are the disclosure and the license terms, and does the community need to rework the document?
